pos: n. (Jerome of Prague, c. 1379–1416, Czech scholar and friend of Jan Hus, who carried Wycliffe's writings from Oxford to Bohemia, recanted under duress at Constance, withdrew his recantation, and was burned in 1416)
etymology: Known in Czech by the name of his city. Not to be confused with Jerome the translator of the Vulgate.
biblical_def: Jerome of Prague was a brilliant and restless master of arts who studied at Oxford, copied Wycliffe's theological works and brought them home, where they shaped the preaching of his friend Hus. When Hus was arrested at the Council of Constance, Jerome went there to support him, was seized, and after months in chains recanted in September 1415, approving the condemnation of Wycliffe and Hus. The recantation gave him no peace. In May 1416, before the council, he withdrew it, declared that nothing he had done in his life grieved him so much as that denial, and affirmed Hus a good and holy man. His fall and recovery were Peter's: Peter denied, “And Peter went out, and wept bitterly” (Luk 22:62), and was restored to confess the same Lord before rulers. Jerome now spoke like the psalmist, “I will speak of thy testimonies also before kings, and will not be ashamed” (Psa 119:46). He was burned on 30 May 1416. A papal secretary who watched, the humanist Poggio Bracciolini, wrote that no Stoic ever met death with so steady a mind. Christ's word sustained him: “fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul” (Mat 10:28); “be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life” (Rev 2:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines recantation as the act of recanting; a declaration that contradicts a former one; retraction; a renunciation of opinions.
webster_full: RECANTATION, n. The act of recanting; a declaration that contradicts a former one.
scriptures: And Peter went out, and wept bitterly.
I will speak of thy testimonies also before kings, and will not be ashamed.
And fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell.
Rev 2:10

Fear none of those things which thou shalt suffer: behold, the devil shall cast some of you into prison, that ye may be tried; and ye shall have tribulation ten days: be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life.
corruption_summary: Jerome's recantation and its withdrawal show that a believer may fall under terror and be restored, against both the despair that says one denial is final and the comfort that says denial under pressure does not matter.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern Christians in the West rarely face the stake, but they face the same choice in milder forms: to say what the authorities, the employer or the culture require, and keep the faith privately. The usual comfort is that coerced words do not count. Jerome knew better. The recantation he made in chains was the heaviest sin of his life to him, and he could not rest until he had withdrawn it publicly at the cost of his life.

The other error is despair. A man who has denied Christ under pressure may think himself beyond recovery. Peter and Jerome both answer it. The recovery is repentance as public as the fall, and the confidence that the Lord who looked on Peter restores those who weep bitterly and return to confess Him.
roots_summary: Greek klaio (G2799), to weep; Hebrew edah (H5713), testimony; Greek pistos (G4103), faithful.
usage: “Peter went out, and wept bitterly” (Luk 22:62) — the fall Jerome repented of.
“I will speak of thy testimonies also before kings” (Psa 119:46) — his withdrawal before the council.
“be thou faithful unto death” (Rev 2:10) — the stake at Constance, 1416.

pos: n. (Patrick Hamilton, 1504–1528, first preacher and martyr of the Scottish Reformation, burned at St Andrews at the age of twenty-four)
etymology: Scottish personal name. His short Latin theses on law and gospel, translated by John Frith, are known as Patrick's Places.
biblical_def: Patrick Hamilton was of royal blood, titular abbot of Fearn, and a student at Paris and Louvain when Luther's writings were first being read. Returning to St Andrews he preached justification by faith, fled to Germany when the archbishop moved against him, studied at the new Protestant university of Marburg, and there wrote his Places, a set of propositions distinguishing the law, which shows sin, from the gospel, which shows Christ. Their burden is Paul's: “by the deeds of the law there shall no flesh be justified in his sight: for by the law is the knowledge of sin” (Rom 3:20), and “a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law” (Rom 3:28). He went back to Scotland knowing what it would cost. Invited to a conference at St Andrews, he was condemned and burned before St Salvator's College on 29 February 1528; the fire was badly made and he suffered for some six hours. His last words, like Stephen's, were “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit” (Act 7:59). A contemporary remarked to the archbishop that if he burned any more he should burn them in cellars, for the smoke of Master Patrick Hamilton had infected as many as it blew upon.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines martyr as one who, by his death, bears witness to the truth of the gospel; and, in a general sense, one who suffers death in defence of any cause.
webster_full: MARTYR, n. One who, by his death, bears witness to the truth of the gospel.
2. One who suffers death in defence of any cause.
scriptures: Rom 3:20
Therefore by the deeds of the law there shall no flesh be justified in his sight: for by the law is the knowledge of sin.
Rom 3:28
Therefore we conclude that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law.
Gal 2:16

Knowing that a man is not justified by the works of the law, but by the faith of Jesus Christ, even we have believed in Jesus Christ, that we might be justified by the faith of Christ, and not by the works of the law: for by the works of the law shall no flesh be justified.
Act 7:59
And they stoned Stephen, calling upon God, and saying, Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.
corruption_summary: Hamilton died for the distinction between law and gospel, which the modern church has largely dissolved into a single message of moral improvement with Christ as helper.
corruption_paragraphs: The Places turn on a simple contrast: the law says, Pay what thou owest; the gospel says, Christ hath paid it. Much modern preaching collapses the two, preaching the gospel as a programme of life change and the law as good advice, so that hearers never despair of themselves and never rest in Christ. That is the medieval confusion Hamilton came home to oppose, and it has returned in evangelical dress.

The recovery is to preach the law in its full severity, to shut every mouth, and the gospel in its full freeness, to open every hand. A young man burned for six hours at St Andrews because he would not blur that line; the smoke of it carried the Reformation through Scotland.
roots_summary: Greek dikaioo (G1344), to justify; ergon (G2041), work, deed; epignosis (G1922), knowledge.
roots_lines: Greek dikaioo (G1344) — to declare righteous; Romans 3:20, 28, Galatians 2:16.
usage: “by the law is the knowledge of sin” (Rom 3:20) — the first half of Patrick's Places.
“a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law” (Rom 3:28) — the second half.
“Lord Jesus, receive my spirit” (Act 7:59) — his words at the stake.

pos: n. (Thomas Bilney, c. 1495–1531, Cambridge scholar converted by reading 1 Timothy 1:15 in Erasmus's Greek Testament, the means of Hugh Latimer's conversion, burned at Norwich)
etymology: English surname. Called ‘Little Bilney’ by his friends for his slight build.
biblical_def: Thomas Bilney was a young fellow of Trinity Hall, Cambridge, worn out by penances that gave no peace, when he bought Erasmus's new Latin and Greek Testament for its style and came on Paul's sentence: “This is a faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptation, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief” (1Ti 1:15). He wrote later that the words gave such comfort that his bruised bones leapt for joy. He gathered the little company at the White Horse inn that became the seedbed of the English Reformation, and he made his confession to the priest Hugh Latimer — in order, as it turned out, to convert him. Arrested in 1527, he abjured under pressure and fell into a long misery of conscience. In 1531 he went out to preach again in Norfolk, saying he must go up to Jerusalem, was condemned, and was burned at Norwich in August. The night before, it is recorded, he held his finger in a candle flame and spoke of Isaiah's promise: “when thou walkest through the fire, thou shalt not be burned; neither shall the flame kindle upon thee” (Isa 43:2), which he took of the soul, not the body.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines comfort as relief from pain; ease; rest or moderate pleasure after pain, cold or distress; support; consolation under calamity.
webster_full: COMFORT, n. Relief from pain; ease; rest or moderate pleasure after pain, cold or distress.
2. Support; consolation under calamity, distress or danger.
3. That which gives strength or support in distress.
scriptures: This is a faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptation, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief.
Isa 43:2

When thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee; and through the rivers, they shall not overflow thee: when thou walkest through the fire, thou shalt not be burned; neither shall the flame kindle upon thee.
Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.
I will speak of thy testimonies also before kings, and will not be ashamed.
corruption_summary: Bilney's conversion is a model of the gospel's comfort to an afflicted conscience, and his long misery after abjuring warns that a conscience cannot be quieted by a lie told to save the body.
corruption_paragraphs: The medieval church offered the troubled conscience penances, masses and indulgences, and Bilney spent himself on them without peace. Modern culture offers therapy and self-acceptance to the same end, and with the same result: the conscience is managed rather than answered. One verse answered Bilney's because it spoke of Christ, not of him: Christ came to save sinners, and the chief of them.

His fall afterward is part of the lesson. He abjured to escape the fire and found the conscience a worse fire. The recovery is the whole of his story — the free mercy that saves the chief of sinners, and the courage that mercy gives to confess Christ openly at last.
roots_summary: Greek pistos (G4103), faithful; apodoche (G594), acceptation; Hebrew kawah (H3554), to burn, scorch.
roots_lines: Greek pistos logos — a faithful saying; 1 Timothy 1:15, 4:9, 2 Timothy 2:11, Titus 3:8.
Hebrew kawah (H3554) — to burn, be scorched; Isaiah 43:2.
usage: “Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners” (1Ti 1:15) — the verse that converted Bilney.
“when thou walkest through the fire, thou shalt not be burned” (Isa 43:2) — his text on the night before Norwich.
“Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden” (Mat 11:28) — the rest his penances never gave.

pos: n. (John Frith, 1503–1533, Cambridge scholar and fellow-labourer of Tyndale, who wrote against purgatory and the corporal presence and was burned at Smithfield at thirty)
etymology: English surname. Translator of Patrick Hamilton's Places.
biblical_def: John Frith was one of the most gifted young scholars of Cambridge and Oxford, imprisoned for reading Lutheran books, and on release he joined William Tyndale on the Continent. He wrote A Disputation of Purgatory answering Thomas More and Bishop Fisher, arguing that Christ's blood leaves no remainder of sin to be purged: “the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from all sin” (1Jn 1:7), and “by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified” (Heb 10:14). He also wrote that the corporal presence of Christ in the sacrament is not an article of faith necessary to salvation, since “It is the spirit that quickeneth; the flesh profiteth nothing” (Joh 6:63), and the Supper is to “shew the Lord's death till he come” (1Co 11:26). Returning to England in 1532 he was arrested, examined by More's successors and by Cranmer among others, and refused to recant. He was burned at Smithfield on 4 July 1533 with a young tailor, Andrew Hewet, who said he believed as Frith believed. The wind blew the fire away from him, and he died slowly, praying for his persecutors.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines purgatory as, among Roman Catholics, a place in which souls after death are purified from venial sins, or suffer punishment for mortal sins not fully satisfied for in this life.
webster_full: PURGATORY, n. Among Catholics, a place in which souls after death are supposed to be purified from venial sins, or where they suffer punishment for sins not fully satisfied for in this life.
scriptures: But if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship one with another, and the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from all sin.
For by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified.
Joh 6:63
It is the spirit that quickeneth; the flesh profiteth nothing: the words that I speak unto you, they are spirit, and they are life.
For as often as ye eat this bread, and drink this cup, ye do shew the Lord's death till he come.
corruption_summary: Frith died for the sufficiency of Christ's one offering, the doctrine that purgatory denies and that modern evangelical ecumenism treats as negotiable.
corruption_paragraphs: Purgatory rests on the premise that Christ's death removes the guilt of sin but leaves a temporal punishment to be paid by the believer, in this life or the next. Frith saw that the premise contradicts the gospel: if the blood cleanses from all sin and one offering perfects for ever, nothing remains to be purged. Recent ecumenical statements on justification have tended to pass over purgatory and indulgences as secondary. They are not secondary; they are the logic of a gospel in which Christ's work is incomplete.

The recovery is Hebrews 10: a finished sacrifice, a perfected people, and no further offering for sin. The 1689 Confession confesses that the souls of the righteous are at death received into the highest heavens, and that Scripture acknowledges no place besides heaven and hell.
roots_summary: Greek katharizo (G2511), to cleanse; teleioo (G5048), to perfect; prosphora (G4376), offering.
roots_lines: Greek katharizo (G2511) — to make clean, purge; 1 John 1:7, 9.
usage: “cleanseth us from all sin” (1Jn 1:7) — Frith's answer to purgatory.
“by one offering he hath perfected for ever” (Heb 10:14) — nothing left to purge.
“the flesh profiteth nothing” (Joh 6:63) — his answer on the corporal presence.

pos: n. (John Hooper, c. 1495–1555, bishop of Gloucester and Worcester, the first English opponent of clerical vestments, burned at Gloucester under Mary)
etymology: English surname. Called the father of Nonconformity for his stand against the vestments in 1550.
biblical_def: John Hooper was a Cistercian monk who came to the Reformed faith through Zwingli and Bullinger, lived in exile at Zurich, and returned under Edward VI as a fiery preacher. Named bishop of Gloucester in 1550, he refused to be consecrated in the prescribed vestments, arguing that garments borrowed from the Roman priesthood had no warrant in Scripture and taught the people the old error. His principle was Christ's: “in vain they do worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men” (Mat 15:9). He was imprisoned in the Fleet for it and at last yielded for the occasion, but he had raised the question the Puritans would carry for a century. As bishop he was tireless, examining his clergy and finding many who could not say who was the author of the Lord's Prayer; he sought to be what Paul required: “A bishop then must be blameless, the husband of one wife, vigilant, sober, of good behaviour, given to hospitality, apt to teach” (1Ti 3:2). Under Mary he was deprived, imprisoned, and burned at Gloucester on 9 February 1555 before his own cathedral. The fire was green and the wind contrary, and he burned for three quarters of an hour. Hebrews speaks of such: “others had trial of cruel mockings and scourgings, yea, moreover of bonds and imprisonment” (Heb 11:36).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines vestment as a garment; some part of clothing or dress; especially some part of outer clothing, as the vestments of the priests.
webster_full: VESTMENT, n. A garment; some part of clothing or dress; especially, some part of outer clothing; as the vestments of the priests.
scriptures: Mat 15:9
But in vain they do worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men.
A bishop then must be blameless, the husband of one wife, vigilant, sober, of good behaviour, given to hospitality, apt to teach;
And others had trial of cruel mockings and scourgings, yea, moreover of bonds and imprisonment:

But none of these things move me, neither count I my life dear unto myself, so that I might finish my course with joy, and the ministry, which I have received of the Lord Jesus, to testify the gospel of the grace of God.
corruption_summary: Hooper's quarrel over vestments is dismissed as fussiness about clothes; it was the first English statement of the regulative principle, that worship is governed by what God commands.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern Christians tend to regard the vestiarian controversy as an embarrassing distraction, as though a bishop risked prison over a surplice. Hooper's point was not taste but authority: who has the right to add ceremonies to the worship of God? If the church may impose garments that signify a sacrificing priesthood, it may impose anything, and the people learn from the clothes what the sermon denies.

The recovery is the principle, now confessed in the 1689 Confession, that the acceptable way of worshipping the true God is instituted by Himself and limited by His own revealed will, so that He may not be worshipped according to the imaginations and devices of men. Hooper lost the battle over the rochet and won the argument for a century of Puritans.
roots_summary: Greek maten (G3155), in vain; nephalios (G3524), vigilant, sober; empaigmos (G1701), mocking.
roots_lines: Greek maten (G3155) — in vain, to no purpose; Matthew 15:9.
usage: “teaching for doctrines the commandments of men” (Mat 15:9) — Hooper's case against the vestments.
“A bishop then must be blameless” (1Ti 3:2) — the standard he set his clergy.
“neither count I my life dear unto myself” (Act 20:24) — the fire at Gloucester.

pos: n. (John Bradford, c. 1510–1555, converted lawyer, prebendary of St Paul's and chaplain to Ridley, burned at Smithfield under Mary)
etymology: English surname. His prison letters and meditations were among the most loved devotional writings of the English Reformation.
biblical_def: John Bradford was a paymaster's clerk in Henry VIII's army who, on his conversion, discovered that his master had defrauded the king and would not rest until restitution was made, as Zacchaeus said, “if I have taken any thing from any man by false accusation, I restore him fourfold” (Luk 19:8). He went up to Cambridge, became a Reformed preacher and one of Edward VI's chaplains, and was imprisoned within weeks of Mary's accession. In prison he wrote letters and meditations of great tenderness and preached to the prisoners. The saying ‘There, but for the grace of God, goes John Bradford’ is traditionally attributed to him on seeing criminals led to execution; its sense is Paul's: “by the grace of God I am what I am” (1Co 15:10). He was burned at Smithfield on 1 July 1555 with John Leaf, a young apprentice. At the stake he turned to the boy and told him to be of good comfort, for they would have a merry supper with the Lord that night, as John was told, “Blessed are they which are called unto the marriage supper of the Lamb” (Rev 19:9). His last words were of the narrow way: “strait is the gate, and narrow is the way, which leadeth unto life, and few there be that find it” (Mat 7:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines restitution as the act of returning or restoring to a person some thing or right of which he has been unjustly deprived.
webster_full: RESTITUTION, n. The act of returning or restoring to a person some thing or right of which he has been unjustly deprived.
2. The act of making good, or of giving an equivalent for any loss, damage or injury; indemnification.
scriptures: Luk 19:8
And Zacchaeus stood, and said unto the Lord; Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor; and if I have taken any thing from any man by false accusation, I restore him fourfold.
But by the grace of God I am what I am: and his grace which was bestowed upon me was not in vain; but I laboured more abundantly than they all: yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me.
Mat 7:14
Because strait is the gate, and narrow is the way, which leadeth unto life, and few there be that find it.
Rev 19:9
And he saith unto me, Write, Blessed are they which are called unto the marriage supper of the Lamb. And he saith unto me, These are the true sayings of God.
corruption_summary: The saying attributed to Bradford has become a cliché of humility; in his mouth it was a confession of sovereign grace, and his restitution is the forgotten half of his conversion.
corruption_paragraphs: ‘There but for the grace of God’ is now said about luck, circumstance or privilege. For Bradford it meant that the only difference between himself and the condemned man was God's free grace, not his own goodness — the doctrine of election in a sentence, which modern use has emptied of God. The other half of his story is equally out of fashion: a converted man who insisted on repaying what had been stolen, though the fraud was not his own, because repentance that keeps the profits of sin is not repentance.

The recovery is to put both back together: grace that alone distinguishes one sinner from another, and repentance that restores what was taken. Bradford died, as he lived, a debtor to grace who had paid his debts to men.
roots_summary: Greek apodidomi (G591), to restore; charis (G5485), grace; stenos (G4728), strait, narrow.
roots_lines: Greek apodidomi (G591) — to give back, restore; Luke 19:8.
usage: “I restore him fourfold” (Luk 19:8) — the first fruit of Bradford's conversion.
“by the grace of God I am what I am” (1Co 15:10) — the meaning of the saying.
“strait is the gate, and narrow is the way” (Mat 7:14) — his last words at Smithfield.

pos: n. (Gottschalk of Orbais, c. 808–c. 868, Saxon monk who taught a twofold predestination from Augustine and was condemned, flogged and imprisoned for the last twenty years of his life)
biblical_def: Gottschalk was given to the monastery of Fulda as a child by his father, sought release as a young man and was refused, and turned to the study of Augustine with an intensity that made him the most controversial theologian of his century. He taught that predestination is twofold: God has predestined the elect to life and the reprobate to death, the one by grace and the other by justice. Paul is the root of it: “whom he did predestinate, them he also called: and whom he called, them he also justified: and whom he justified, them he also glorified” (Rom 8:30), and “hath he mercy on whom he will have mercy, and whom he will he hardeneth” (Rom 9:18). He also denied that Christ died with intent to save the reprobate, citing Christ's words, “ye believe not, because ye are not of my sheep” (Joh 10:26). Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, had him condemned at Mainz in 848 and at Quierzy in 849, flogged until he threw his writings into the fire, and shut up in the monastery of Hautvillers, where he died some twenty years later, refusing the last rites rather than recant. Several bishops, Prudentius of Troyes and Ratramnus among them, defended his doctrine.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines predestination as the act of decreeing or foreordaining events; and, in theology, the decree of God by which he hath from eternity unchangeably appointed or determined whatever comes to pass.
webster_full: PREDESTINATION, n. The act of decreeing or foreordaining events.
2. In theology, the decree of God by which he hath, from eternity, unchangeably appointed or determined whatever comes to pass; used particularly in reference to the salvation of men.
scriptures: Rom 8:29
For whom he did foreknow, he also did predestinate to be conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brethren.
Rom 8:30
Moreover whom he did predestinate, them he also called: and whom he called, them he also justified: and whom he justified, them he also glorified.
Rom 9:18
Therefore hath he mercy on whom he will have mercy, and whom he will he hardeneth.
But ye believe not, because ye are not of my sheep, as I said unto you.
corruption_summary: Gottschalk's condemnation shows how quickly the church that honoured Augustine abandoned his doctrine of grace, and how the same abandonment now passes for mainstream evangelical theology.
corruption_paragraphs: The ninth-century bishops who condemned Gottschalk professed to follow Augustine, but they taught a predestination based on foreseen merits and a God who wills all men to be saved in the same way, with the decisive difference supplied by man. That is the semi-Pelagian settlement that the medieval church lived in, and it is substantially the position of most evangelicals today, who confess election in name and explain it as God's foresight of human choice.

The Reformed confess the Augustinian doctrine Gottschalk suffered for, with the care of the 1689 Confession: some men and angels are predestinated unto eternal life through Jesus Christ, to the praise of His glorious grace; others are left to act in their sin to their just condemnation, to the praise of His glorious justice. He was a difficult man, and his manner did not help him; his doctrine was Paul's.
roots_summary: Greek proorizo (G4309), to predestinate; proginosko (G4267), to foreknow; skleruno (G4645), to harden.
roots_lines: Greek proorizo (G4309) — to determine beforehand; Romans 8:29–30, Ephesians 1:5, 11.
Greek proginosko (G4267) — to know beforehand, foreknow; Romans 8:29, 11:2.
usage: “whom he did predestinate, them he also called” (Rom 8:30) — Gottschalk's golden chain.
“whom he will he hardeneth” (Rom 9:18) — the half of his doctrine the bishops could not bear.
“ye are not of my sheep” (Joh 10:26) — his text on the extent of Christ's saving intent.

pos: n. (Thomas Bradwardine, c. 1300–1349, Oxford mathematician and theologian, the ‘Profound Doctor,’ author of The Cause of God against the Pelagians, archbishop of Canterbury for a few weeks before dying of the plague)
etymology: English surname. His De causa Dei contra Pelagium appeared in 1344.
biblical_def: Thomas Bradwardine was a fellow of Merton College, Oxford, a pioneer of mathematical physics, and confessor to Edward III on campaign. He tells how, as a young student, he thought himself a Pelagian, believing that a man's own free will made him worthy of grace, until reading Paul he was struck by the words, “it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy” (Rom 9:16). From that came his great book The Cause of God, a vast defence of the sovereignty of grace against the ‘modern Pelagians’ of the Oxford schools, who taught that a man doing what is in him would receive grace as a fitting reward. His charge against them was Paul's question: “what hast thou that thou didst not receive? now if thou didst receive it, why dost thou glory, as if thou hadst not received it?” (1Co 4:7). God is He “who worketh all things after the counsel of his own will” (Eph 1:11). Chosen archbishop of Canterbury in 1349, he died of the Black Death some five weeks after his consecration. His book was read by Wycliffe, and his witness stands among the medieval voices that kept Augustine's doctrine of grace alive until the Reformation.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines sovereignty as supreme power; supremacy; the possession of the highest power, or of uncontrollable power.
webster_full: SOVEREIGNTY, n. Supreme power; supremacy; the possession of the highest power, or of uncontrollable power.
2. Absolute sovereignty belongs only to God.
scriptures: Rom 9:16
So then it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy.
For who maketh thee to differ from another? and what hast thou that thou didst not receive? now if thou didst receive it, why dost thou glory, as if thou hadst not received it?
Eph 1:11
In whom also we have obtained an inheritance, being predestinated according to the purpose of him who worketh all things after the counsel of his own will:
Php 2:13
For it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do of his good pleasure.
corruption_summary: Bradwardine's ‘modern Pelagians’ taught that God gives grace to those who do their best, and that teaching is now the working theology of most popular preaching.
corruption_paragraphs: The late-medieval maxim was that God will not deny grace to the man who does what is in him. It sounds pious and fair: God meets the sincere seeker halfway. Bradwardine saw that it makes the first move man's and turns grace into a reward. The same idea fills modern evangelism and devotional writing, in which God waits on the sinner's decision and blesses the effort of the willing.

The recovery is Bradwardine's text. Salvation is not of him that willeth; every good thing the believer has, he received; and God works all things after the counsel of His own will. A mathematician at Oxford reasoned his way back to Paul, and his reasoning passed through Wycliffe into the Reformation.
roots_summary: Greek trecho (G5143), to run; kauchaomai (G2744), to glory, boast; boule (G1012), counsel.
usage: “it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth” (Rom 9:16) — the verse that undid Bradwardine's Pelagianism.
“what hast thou that thou didst not receive?” (1Co 4:7) — his question to the schools.
“who worketh all things after the counsel of his own will” (Eph 1:11) — the cause of God.

pos: n. pl. (the Waldenses or Waldensians, the movement begun by Valdes of Lyons in the 1170s, which preached the Scriptures in the common tongue, survived centuries of persecution in the Alpine valleys, and joined the Reformation in 1532)
etymology: From Valdes (later called Peter Waldo), the merchant of Lyons who founded the movement. Also called the Poor Men of Lyons.
biblical_def: The Waldenses began with a rich merchant of Lyons who had portions of Scripture translated into the Provençal tongue, gave away his goods, and began to preach. Forbidden by the archbishop and then by the pope, the Poor Men of Lyons answered with the apostles: “we cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard” (Act 4:20). They were condemned at Verona in 1184 and hunted by the Inquisition, and like the persecuted church of Acts, “they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word” (Act 8:4). They memorised whole books of the Bible, rejected purgatory, prayers for the dead and the authority of unworthy priests, and survived above all in the valleys of Piedmont. At the synod of Chanforan in 1532 they joined the Reformed churches, and paid for Olivétan's French Bible of 1535, from which Calvin's Geneva Bible descended. In 1655 the Duke of Savoy's troops massacred them in the Piedmont Easter, and Milton wrote his sonnet beginning ‘Avenge, O Lord, thy slaughtered saints.’ It is the cry under the altar: “How long, O Lord, holy and true, dost thou not judge and avenge our blood on them that dwell on the earth?” (Rev 6:10).

webster_full: VERNACULAR, a. Belonging to the country of one's birth; one's own by birth or nature; native.
2. The vernacular language of a country is the native tongue.

corruption_summary: The Waldenses are claimed as an unbroken Protestant church from the apostles; the honest record is better — a lay Bible movement that endured persecution for three centuries and then received the Reformation as its own.
corruption_paragraphs: Older Protestant writers, seeking an answer to Rome's question ‘Where was your church before Luther?’, sometimes made the Waldenses into an apostolic succession of pure churches reaching back to the first century. The historical record does not support the claim, and Reformed readers do not need it. The church's continuity is in the Word and the faith, not in an unbroken institution; the Waldenses are precious because they kept the Word among the poor when the institution would not.

The recovery is their actual witness: Scripture in the people's tongue, memorised by farmers and taught by itinerants; obedience to God rather than men; and a willingness to merge their old ways into the Reformed churches when the fuller light came. Their valleys are a monument to what the Bible in plain hands can do.

pos: n. pl. (the English followers of John Wycliffe in the late fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, who read and copied the Scriptures in English and were persecuted under the statute for the burning of heretics)
etymology: Middle Dutch lollaerd, a mumbler of prayers, a term of contempt; applied in England to Wycliffe's followers from the 1380s.
biblical_def: The Lollards carried Wycliffe's teaching out of Oxford into the towns and villages of England. Their chief treasure was the English Bible translated by Wycliffe's circle, copied by hand in hundreds of manuscripts, many of them small enough to hide, and read aloud in households at night. They obeyed the apostle: “Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom” (Col 3:16), and the law's charge to fathers, “thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children” (Deu 6:7). Their Twelve Conclusions, fixed to the doors of Westminster Hall in 1395, attacked clerical celibacy, transubstantiation, pilgrimages and the worship of images. Parliament answered in 1401 with the statute for the burning of heretics, and in 1409 Archbishop Arundel forbade any English translation of Scripture to be made or read without a bishop's licence. Lollards were burned, and many recanted; but the movement survived underground in families until the 1520s, when Tyndale's printed Testament reached men and women who had been reading the Wycliffe Bible in secret for generations. They lived by Christ's word: “Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me” (Joh 5:39).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines Lollard as a name given to the followers of Wickliffe in England; a sect of early reformers.
webster_full: LOLLARD, n. A name given to the followers of Wickliffe, or a sect of early reformers in Germany and England.
LOLLARDY, n. The doctrines of the Lollards.

Joh 5:39

And that from a child thou hast known the holy scriptures, which are able to make thee wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus.
corruption_summary: The Lollards' crime was reading the Bible in English; a church that prizes access to Scripture now neglects the reading that men and women once risked the fire to do.
corruption_paragraphs: The Constitutions of Arundel made it a crime to own or read an unlicensed English Scripture, and men were burned with English Gospels hung about their necks. The modern English-speaking Christian has more Bibles than any people in history and reads them less than the Lollard families did by candlelight. Scripture memory, family reading and the copying of the text by hand were the habits that kept the faith alive for a hundred and thirty years without a single church building of their own.

The recovery is not nostalgia but practice: the Word read aloud in households, taught to children from their earliest years as Timothy was taught (2Ti 3:15), and treasured as a thing worth dying for. The Lollards did not have the Reformation's full theology, but they had the book, and the book brought the Reformation.
